{{Short description|Australian cryptography policy review}}

The '''Walsh Report''' was an Australian cryptography policy review undertaken for the Australian government by Gerard Walsh, initially released in 1996 and then withdrawn before its sale to the public. [[Electronic Frontiers Australia]] (EFA) obtained a redacted copy under [[Freedom of Information Act 1982|freedom of information laws]] and published it on EFA's website. Subsequently, an unredacted copy was found and the redacted parts were added to the EFA copy.

==Policy review==

The Walsh Report was an Australian cryptography policy review undertaken at the request of the Secretary of the [[Attorney-General's Department (Australia)|Attorney-General's Department]]<ref name=Ellsmore99>{{cite web
|first1=Nick
|last1=Ellsmore
|url=http://cryptome.org/crypto97-ne.htm
|title=Cryptology: Law Enforcement & National Security vs. Privacy, Security & The Future of Commerce.
|website=cryptome.org/
|date=4 July 1999
|accessdate=25 August 2014
}}</ref> by Gerard Walsh, the former deputy director of the [[Australian Security Intelligence Organisation]] (ASIO).<ref name=EPIC99>{{cite book
|title=Cryptography And Liberty 1999: An International Survey of Encryption Policy
|date=1999
|publisher=Electronic Privacy Information Center
|isbn=1893044033
|url=http://gilc.org/crypto/crypto-survey-99.html
|accessdate=10 July 2014
}}</ref> The report included a broad analysis of cryptography issues from an Australian context.<ref name=Koops98>{{cite book
|first1=Bert-Jaap
|last1=Koops
|title=The Crypto Controversy: A Key Conflict in the Information Society
|date=1998
|publisher=Kluwer Law International
|isbn=9041111433
|page=2
|url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=9041111433&dq=%22electronic+frontiers+australia%22
|accessdate=22 June 2014
}}</ref>

The report, titled ''Review of Policy relating to Encryption Technologies'', is popularly called the Walsh Report.<ref name=EPIC99/>

In his report, Walsh found that there was a lack of coordination in the government over the establishment of cryptography policy. Walsh also reported no clarity as to which department and which minister was responsible for cryptographic policy. Consequently, there was a danger that policy would be developed without being coordinated.<ref name=EPIC99/>

The main advice given by Walsh in the report was that major legislative action to safeguard law-enforcement or national security was not required at the time.

No specific options were recommended in the report for legislation on cryptography, nor did the report recommend mandatory key recovery.<ref name=Koops13>{{cite web
|first1=Bert-Jaap
|last1=Koops
|url=http://www.cryptolaw.org/cls2.htm#aus
|title=Crypto Law Survey : Australia
|website=cryptolaw.org/
|date=February 2013
|accessdate=25 August 2014
}}</ref>

Recommendations in the report for minor legislative and other actions included:
* establishment of a summary law on intrusive investigative powers
* to consider the setting up of an additional and more serious offence when cryptography is used to obstruct a criminal investigation
* to consider establishing a power to allow police to demand encryption keys<ref name=Koops13/>
* a key recovery or [[Key escrow|escrow]] scheme, as had been advocated by the United States, not be established by Australia.<ref name=EPIC99/>

==History==

===Background===

Walsh was invited to undertake his review following on from the [[Barrett Report (Australia)|Barrett Report]], which concluded: "while Australian agencies all report that encryption has not been a problem to date, it is likely to become one in the future."<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

===Initial issue===

The Walsh Report was issued on 10 October 1996.<ref name=EPIC99/>

===Deposit copies===

After being printed, deposit copies of the report were lodged by the [[Australian Government Publishing Service]] (AGPS)<ref name=EU99>{{cite news
|title=Australia - Walsh report on global cryptography debate
|url=http://www2.echo.lu/legal/en/news/9901/chapter11.html#1
|accessdate=22 August 2014
|work=EU Legal Advisory Board News
|date=January–February 1999
|quote=In December 1998, several uncensored copies of the Walsh Report, which constitutes an important review of Australian cryptography policy, were found in public and university libraries in Australia. These are believed to be deposit copies lodged by the Australian Government Publishing Service (AGPS) after the report was printed but before the 1997 decision by the Attorney-General's Department to withhold it from commercial sale. In March 1997, Electronic Frontiers Australia (EFA), applied for release of the report under the 1982 Freedom of Information Act.
}} {{Dead link|date=July 2017}}</ref> with around 40 university and public libraries under a free deposit scheme.<ref name=Tebbutt99>{{cite news
|first1=Dan
|last1=Tebbutt
|title=Canberra suppresses IT report
|url=http://technology.news.com.au/techno/4186000.htm
|accessdate=20 August 2014
|work=news.com.au
|date=23 Feb 1999
|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/19990427024303/http://technology.news.com.au/techno/4186000.htm
|archivedate=1999-04-27
}}</ref>

===Embargo===

The report was listed for sale in January 1997 by AGPS. Three weeks later, Electronic Frontiers Australia (EFA) enquired why it was not actually available.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

In February 1997,<ref name=Koops13/> before the Walsh Report was publicly released, the Australian Attorney-General's Department embargoed it and withheld the report from commercial sale.<ref name=EPIC99/><ref name=EU99/>

===FOI request===
In March 1997 EFA applied for the release of the Walsh Report under the [[Freedom of Information Act 1982]].<ref name=Ellsmore99/><ref name=EU99/><ref name=Yiacoumi99>{{cite news
|first1=Roulla
|last1=Yiacoumi
|title=Hidden report reveals crypto paranoia
|url=http://newswire.com.au/9901/crypto.htm
|accessdate=22 August 2014
|work=APC Newswire
|date=13 January 1999
|quote=A university student in Tasmania has stumbled across a pivotal government report on cryptography which was mysteriously withdrawn from public view two years ago. ... Online civil liberties group Electronic Frontiers Australia applied for the report's release under the Freedom of Information Act in March 1997.
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000818091610/http://newswire.com.au/9901/crypto.htm
|archive-date=18 August 2000
|url-status=dead
}}</ref><ref name=Jackson01>{{cite book
|first1=Margaret
|last1=Jackson
|first2=Gordon
|last2=Hughes
|title=Hughes on data protection in Australia
|date=2001
|publisher=Lawbook Company
|isbn=0455217270
|page=319
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8Xw_AQAAIAAJ&dq=%22electronic+frontiers+australia%22
|accessdate=22 June 2014
}}</ref>

Initially, the request was denied. Following a review that was requested by EFA,<ref name=Ellsmore99/> in June 1997<ref name=Ellsmore99/> EFA obtained a copy of the Walsh Report that had been redacted<ref name=EPIC99/><ref name=Koops98/> on national security,<ref name=Koops98/> defence, international relations, internal working document, law enforcement and public safety grounds.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

EFA then published the redacted version of the Walsh Report on its website.<ref name=Jackson01/>

===Discovery of deposit copies===

In December 1998<ref name=EU99/> an uncensored copy of the Walsh Report was discovered in the [[State Library of Tasmania]] by Nick Ellsmore, a university student in Hobart.<ref name=EPIC99/><ref name=Tebbutt99/><ref name=Yiacoumi99/><ref name=aic99>{{cite news
|title=Censored Report Recommends Australian Police Hack Web Sites
|url=http://australia.internet.com/aus-news/1999/01/0401-censored.html
|accessdate=22 August 2014
|work=australia.internet.com
|date=4 January 1999
|quote=Law enforcement agencies in Australia ought to be able to "hack" into corporate computer systems and change proprietary software to enable monitoring of communications, according to a 1996 report which had been censored by the Australian government but recently uncovered by a university student.
}}</ref><ref name=Rogers99>{{cite news
|first1=Matthew
|last1=Rogers
|title=Student exposes spying plans
|url=http://technology.news.com.au/techno/4352808.htm
|accessdate=22 August 2014
|work=The Mercury
|date=15 January 1999
|quote=A HOBART university student has unearthed secret Federal Government plans to let Australia's top spy agencies hire computer hackers to break into the PCs of suspects.
}}{{Dead link|date=May 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Ellsmore alerted EFA to the availability of the report.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

===Publication of unredacted version===

By comparing the redacted and unredacted copies it was possible to identify the censored sections of the report.<ref name=aic99/>

EFA added the redacted parts to its copy on the Internet,<ref name=EPIC99/> and highlighted them in red.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

Following the discovery of the uncensored copies of the Walsh report, ''[[The Australian]]'' newspaper revealed the censored recommendations.<ref name=Tebbutt99/> Release of the complete report was also covered by Hobart's ''[[The Mercury (Hobart)|Mercury]]'', Melbourne's ''[[The Sun-Herald|Sun-Herald]]'', ''[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]'', many Internet news sites and radio stations in Perth and Sydney.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

===Recall of deposit copies===

On 10 February 1999, after ''The Australian'''s revelations, the Australian Government Information Service ([[AusInfo]]), the government publisher, wrote to the deposit libraries. The AusInfo letter, said that the "Attorney-General's Department wants all copies recalled" and asked that copies of the report be returned to AusInfo.

A spokesperson for [[Daryl Williams (politician)|Daryl Williams]], the Attorney-General, said that the release of the Walsh report had been discussed with AusInfo, but denied that the Government initiated the recall.

In February 1999, EFA cryptography committee chairman, Greg Taylor, said: "The bumbling attempts to censor the [Walsh] report have only served to focus international attention on it".<ref name=Tebbutt99/>

==Censored parts==

Redacted observations included:
* Encrypted data is being stored and transmitted beyond the visibility or reach of investigative agencies.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>

The censored recommendations included:
* software booby-traps
* PC bugging<ref name=Tebbutt99/>
* that Australian law enforcement agencies be given the power to "hack" corporate computer systems and to alter [[proprietary software]] to allow for the monitoring of communications<ref name=aic99/>
* as strong cryptographic products can be obtained over the Internet, the efficacy of export controls over cryptographic products as a defensive strategy is dubious<ref name=EPIC99/>
* the conclusion of the Barrett Report that the time when encryption becomes a problem for law enforcement and national security agencies is not yet here, but will soon be
* the surveillance powers of ASIO should be extended.<ref name=Ellsmore99/>
